common_name: G.G. Gerbing Azalea (Classic White Southern Indica Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; a white sport of Formosa, G.G. Gerbing grows to similar large dimensions and needs the same generous spacing.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; like other Southern Indian Hybrid azaleas, G.G. Gerbing is a large, vigorous shrub that resents root disturbance once established, so site it with its mature size in mind. A white-flowered sport of the classic 'Formosa' azalea discovered in Florida, G.G. Gerbing produces an overwhelming mid-spring flush of large, pure white, ruffled flowers with a faint chartreuse throat blotch that lights up shaded borders and woodland edges. In zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens it can reach 8–12 feet tall and wide after decades, forming a dense, billowing evergreen mass that anchors older Southern landscapes much as its magenta parent does. Prune only immediately after the spring bloom finishes, since flower buds for next year set on the current season's growth soon after — pruning in fall or winter removes the coming spring's flowers.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; fall planting lets roots establish ahead of the fall–winter bloom season.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun, spacing plants 30–48 inches apart to fill in as a low hedge or foundation planting. Shishi-Gashira is one of the most popular dwarf, compact sasanqua camellias, staying under 4 feet tall and wider than tall, with small, glossy, dense evergreen leaves and semi-double, rose-pink flowers with a light fragrance produced heavily from October into December. Its low, spreading habit fits foundation plantings, low hedges, and small-garden spaces where a full-size camellia would overwhelm, and it tolerates more sun than most camellias, like other sasanqua types. Prune lightly right after bloom if needed to maintain shape; heavy pruning is rarely necessary given its naturally compact form.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Mine-no-Yuki — Japanese for 'snow on the peak' — is a spreading, wider-than-tall sasanqua cultivar valued as much for its billowing, low-mounding habit as for its flowers. It produces an abundance of large, double, pure white flowers with a light fragrance from October through December, set against small, glossy, dark-green leaves on a shrub that spreads readily by layering where lower branches touch the ground. Its arching, informal, spreading form makes it a favorite for espalier, low informal hedges, and large-scale groundcover-like plantings along woodland edges. Prune right after bloom to control spread if a tidier form is wanted, or let it sprawl for a naturalistic look.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; flowers blue in acidic soil (pH below 5.5) and pink in alkaline soil (pH above 6.5), like other macrophylla cultivars.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, and remove spent flower heads through the season to encourage continued rebloom. Part of the Endless Summer collection, Twist-n-Shout is a reblooming lacecap hydrangea that flowers on both old and new wood, producing flat clusters of pink or blue fertile florets ringed by showy sterile ray flowers from early summer through fall, with the deep red-tinged stems adding fall and winter interest after leaf drop. Because it blooms on new growth as well as old, an errant late-frost or a hard pruning does not eliminate the whole season's flowers the way it does on old-wood-only cultivars, making it more forgiving for gardeners uncertain about pruning timing. Keep soil consistently moist — hydrangeas wilt readily in summer heat — and mulch to conserve moisture and moderate soil temperature.

common_name: Ruby Slippers Oakleaf Hydrangea (Compact Red-Aging Oakleaf Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; oakleaf hydrangea is native to Southeastern woodlands and tolerates more shade than mophead types.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, in a spot sheltered from harsh afternoon sun in the Deep South. Bred at the U.S. National Arboretum, Ruby Slippers is a compact selection of the Southeastern native oakleaf hydrangea, reaching only about 3–4 feet tall and wide — roughly half the size of the species — while still producing large, upright panicles of white flowers that age quickly to deep rose-red by midsummer, holding that color for weeks. Its bold, deeply lobed, oak-shaped leaves turn burgundy to mahogany in fall, and the exfoliating cinnamon bark adds winter interest once leaves drop. Like all oakleaf hydrangeas, it blooms on old wood, so prune only right after flowering, and avoid deep shade, which reduces flowering.

common_name: Snow Queen Oakleaf Hydrangea (Upright Classic Oakleaf Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, allowing room for its full 5–7 foot spread at maturity. A Georgia-bred, Award of Garden Merit-winning selection introduced in the 1960s, Snow Queen is one of the most widely planted oakleaf hydrangea cultivars, valued for its unusually erect, well-branched flower panicles that stand upright rather than nodding, and its heavier-than-average flower production compared to the wild species. Flowers open white in early summer, age to a rich pink-bronze by late summer, and can be left standing through fall and winter for continued interest, while the bold, deeply lobed foliage turns brilliant shades of red, orange, and burgundy in fall before the shrub's cinnamon, exfoliating bark takes over as the winter feature. Blooms form on old wood, so prune, if needed, only in the weeks right after flowering.

common_name: Alice Oakleaf Hydrangea (Large Vigorous Oakleaf Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Alice grows large and needs a spacious woodland-edge or border site.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, giving it the room it needs to reach a mature size of 8–12 feet — one of the largest oakleaf hydrangea cultivars in common cultivation. Selected and introduced by horticulturist Michael Dirr, Alice bears exceptionally large flower panicles, up to 14 inches long, opening white and aging to a soft pinkish-bronze, on a vigorous, coarse-textured shrub with oversized, deeply lobed leaves that turn outstanding shades of orange, red, and purple-bronze in fall. Its scale and bold texture make it a strong specimen or backdrop planting rather than a foundation shrub, and the exfoliating, cinnamon-colored bark provides structure through winter after leaf drop. As with other oakleaf hydrangeas, flower buds form on old wood, so prune only in the weeks immediately following bloom.
